+++ b/minbpe/_heap.py
@@ -55,1 +55,22 @@
-def _build_table(merges):
+def _apply_table(s, table):
+    # s.replace(ps, c) for every (ps, c) of table in order, skipping merges
+    # whose pair cannot occur: present is a superset of the chars of s (a
+    # token only enters s through a replace that shortened it)
+    present = set(s)
+    add = present.add
+    n = len(s)
+    for ps, c, a, b in table:
+        if a in present and b in present:
+            s = s.replace(ps, c)
+            if len(s) != n:
+                n = len(s)
+                add(c)
+    return s
+
+
+def _gated(table):
+    # (ps, c) -> (ps, c, ps[0], ps[1]) for _apply_table
+    return None if table is None else [(ps, c, ps[0], ps[1]) for ps, c in table]
+

+def _build_table(merges):

actions.reason: I tried skipping each merge's str.replace when either of its two tokens is absent from the string, tracked with a set of characters that may be present. Outputs stayed identical, but encode_ir got worse: ratio 1.0129 (366427033 to 371155862). Nearly every merge's tokens are present, so the check only adds per-merge Python overhead. Each replace scans a short string, and that scan is cheap compared with the check. The whole replace loop is only about 4,600 iterations per run, so it is a small share of the roughly 366M instructions. Most of the rest goes to interpreter startup, the regex import and pattern compile, findall, and the benchmark's own corpus generation. I found no library-side change likely to clear the 1% bar (about 3.7M instructions) this session. The repository copy still contains this rejected edit to minbpe/_heap.py; I did not revert it.

journal.text:
I tried to speed up encoding in minbpe/_heap.py by skipping a merge's str.replace whenever either of its two tokens is absent from the string. I tracked presence with a set of characters that may be present. That came to six edits in one file, 37 lines under the guard.

Outputs stayed identical and both builds were fine, but encode_ir got worse: 366427033 to 371155862, ratio 1.0129 against a required 0.9900. train_ir barely moved, 310851172 to 310851166. The outcome was rejected for no_improvement, and I submitted nothing.

My read now is that nearly every merge's tokens are present in the string, so the presence check almost never skips anything. It just adds Python overhead on every merge. Each replace scans a short string, and that scan is already cheap. Pruning per merge on this path is a dead end.

Next time I would reduce the number of Python-level iterations per encoded chunk rather than guard each replace. One way is to batch merges or cache whole chunk results. I would check first what _memo and _chunk_table already cover.
